turns:
=== CALL C0230 ===
Gemma: Hiya! Can you hear me okay? I'm never sure with this laptop, it sort of freezes if Rob's downloading anything.
Rowena: Yes, I can hear you lovely! Hiya, I'm Rowena. You're Gemma, yeah?
Gemma: That's me, yeah. Ooh, I love your glasses. Sorry, that's a weird way to start.
Rowena: No, no, I'll take it! Nobody compliments me at work, they just bleep me. Where are you, then? Are you from round here, wherever here is?
Gemma: Beeston, so just outside Nottingham. Born and bred, really. What about you?
Rowena: Warrington. Great Sankey. But originally from the Philippines, Batangas, I came over in 2003 with the nurse recruitment. Twenty years now, so I'm basically Northern.
Gemma: Oh, you're a nurse? I'm in pharmacy! I'm a pharmacy technician at the hospital in Nottingham.
Rowena: No way! NHS! What do you do, the dispensary?
Gemma: Dispensary mostly, erm, and then I go up on the wards for medicines reconciliation, so sort of checking what people are actually taking at home against what's written down. Which is never the same, do you know what I mean? Someone'll say "oh, I take the little white one" and you're like, right, okay, which little white one, there's about four hundred.
Rowena: [laughs] The little white one! I get that with creams. "The one in the blue tube, love." I'm tissue viability, so pressure ulcers, wounds, that kind of thing.
Gemma: Oh, that's a specialist job, isn't it?
Rowena: Band 7, yeah. I love it, honestly. I do a lot of teaching for the healthcare assistants and the new nurses, and I try to make it fun, because pressure ulcers on a PowerPoint, you know, people's eyes go.
Gemma: I do the training for our new starters! I've got colour-coded checklists, it's a bit of a joke in the department. They call me the highlighter lady.
Rowena: Oh, you'd hate my inbox. It's a disaster. I'd rather go and see a patient than answer an email.
Gemma: [laughs] Fair enough. Erm, sorry, I noticed in your photo, is that a choir rota on your board?
Rowena: Yes! Filipino choir at my parish. We're practising for a fiesta at the minute. Do you sing?
Gemma: I do! Church music group at the Methodist church, I'm an alto, and then a community choir that does pop stuff. We're learning a new one for a summer concert and I keep singing the soprano line by accident.
Rowena: Ah, that's lovely. I knew it, I saw your cross and thought, she'll be a singer.
Gemma: [laughs] That's very good detective work. Is it all hymns, yours, or...
Rowena: Hymns on Sunday, then at the parties it's karaoke, Whitney, Celine. No mercy.
Gemma: Oh, I'd be in tears. I cry at everything. I went to Les Mis at the Theatre Royal and Rob had to give me his sleeve.
Rowena: Me and my work friends do the Palace in Manchester. We saw Wicked and I was a mess. Do you have kids, Gemma?
Gemma: One, Isla, she's six. Dinosaurs and loom bands at the minute. My wrists are covered in them, I look like I've been to a festival.
Rowena: [laughs] I'm the fun auntie. My sister's two, Mia's fifteen, Ethan's eleven. We all live together, it's chaos but nice chaos.
Gemma: Aw, that sounds lovely, actually. My mum does two pick-ups a week for us, I'd be lost without her. Sorry, I'm rambling, aren't I?
Rowena: No, I'm the same! We're going to get told off by the timer. What do you do on a Saturday, then? I always get a barm from the bakery, that's my treat.
Gemma: A barm! See, we'd say cob. A cheese cob from the market.
Rowena: Cob! That sounds like a horse.
Gemma: [laughs] It's a perfectly good word, thank you very much!

=== CALL C0231 ===
Karen: Hello! Oh, sorry, I think I was on mute. Can you hear me now?
Ioana: Yeah, I can hear you.
Karen: Brilliant. I'm Karen. Sorry, I've still got my work lanyard on, I've literally just walked in.
Ioana: That's fine. I'm Ioana.
Karen: Ioana. Lovely name. Where are you, then?
Ioana: Burnt Oak. North West London.
Karen: Oh, not far from me, sort of. I'm Basingstoke. Well, it's not that close, is it, to be honest, it's the M3 and then a nightmare.
Ioana: Yeah, it's a way.
Karen: What do you do? Is that all right to ask? I'm not sure what we're meant to talk about.
Ioana: I think it's whatever. Erm, I'm a lettings administrator. At an estate agent's in Edgware.
Karen: Oh, so tenancies and that?
Ioana: Yeah, tenancy agreements, deposits, gas safety reminders, chasing references. Landlord statements. Basically making sure nobody gets fined.
Karen: That sounds really organised. I'm admin as well, at a building maintenance firm. I book the engineers in, chase invoices, answer the phones. But I'm hopeless, to be fair. My desk is just Post-it notes. I double-booked a plumber last month and he turned up at a job where someone else was already under the sink.
Ioana: [laughs] Okay, that's quite bad.
Karen: It was bad! I owned up, though. My manager just sort of sighed.
Ioana: Honestly, owning up is half of it. The negotiators at mine promise tenants stuff without checking, then it's me who has to sort it. They never say sorry.
Karen: That would wind me up, yeah.
Ioana: It does. I've been told to soften my emails, so.
Karen: [laughs] Soften them how?
Ioana: Like, I wrote to a landlord, "As I said in my previous three emails." And apparently that's passive-aggressive.
Karen: Well, it's a bit aggressive. But he deserved it, probably.
Ioana: He did. He emails me at eleven at night.
Karen: Oh, no. Sorry, where was I? I was going to ask, what do you do when you're not at work? That's probably a boring question, isn't it?
Ioana: No, it's fine. Erm, walking, mostly, at the weekends. Stanmore Common. And I'm doing an accounting course in the evenings, AAT.
Karen: In the evenings? After a full day? I'd be asleep on the settee by eight. I'm knackered most nights, I just put a crime drama on.
Ioana: What are you watching?
Karen: Oh, I'm halfway through this new one, the detective with the dodgy back, I can't remember the name. I binged four episodes Sunday while my son was at his dad's.
Ioana: I watch loads of those. Scandinavian ones especially. My boyfriend talks through them, so I watch them on my own.
Karen: Callum does that! My son, he's fourteen. "Who's that? Is he the killer?" Every five minutes.
Ioana: Yeah, that's Liam. And then he guesses right and he's so smug about it.
Karen: [laughs] Have you seen The Bridge?
Ioana: Yeah, the first two series are really good. Then it kind of goes off.
Karen: I never finished it. I don't really finish anything, to be honest. My mum gives me books and they just sit there.
Ioana: I read on the bus. The 113's always late, so I get loads done.
Karen: Every cloud, eh?

=== CALL C0232 ===
Agnieszka: Hello! Hello, can you see me?
Courtney: Yeah.
Agnieszka: Oh good. I'm Agnieszka. It's a hard one, people say "Agnes" sometimes, it's fine.
Courtney: Courtney.
Agnieszka: Nice to meet you, Courtney. Where are you calling from?
Courtney: Sunderland.
Agnieszka: Oh, far up! I'm in Yeovil, in Somerset. Very different, I think.
Courtney: Probably, yeah.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Okay. Erm, did you do the puzzle bit at the start? I was terrible. I think I was too slow.
Courtney: It was all right. I didn't finish the last one.
Agnieszka: Me also not! Okay, good, so not just me. I'm a care assistant, senior care assistant in a care home, so I'm used to people who can't find their glasses, not puzzles. Sorry, I talk too much, yeah? What do you do?
Courtney: Erm, admin. Lettings office. Phones and that.
Agnieszka: Do you like it?
Courtney: No. It's fine. It pays for stuff.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Honest, I like it.
Courtney: Yeah.
Agnieszka: In your photo, I saw the drawings on the wall behind you. Are they yours?
Courtney: Erm... yeah. Most of them.
Agnieszka: They looked very detailed, even small on the screen. What do you draw?
Courtney: It's kind of ink stuff, like, fineliner. Hands a lot. Moths. Faces that sort of turn into plants, like the skin goes into leaves and roots. People say it's creepy but I don't think it is, it's more like, things changing into other things. I've been doing hands for months because they're dead hard, there's loads going on in them, all the little lines and the knuckles, and if you get one bit wrong the whole thing looks like a glove. I've got this new pen, it's a point oh three, and it's... sorry. I'm going on.
Agnieszka: No, no, I like it! You know, at work I see a lot of hands. Old hands, very thin skin, all the lines. One lady, she is ninety-four, her hands are like a map. I always think somebody should draw them.
Courtney: That's actually... yeah. Old hands are the best ones to draw. My nana let me draw hers once.
Agnieszka: Ah, bless her. You're close to your nana?
Courtney: Yeah. She lives two streets away. She's the one who got me drawing, really.
Agnieszka: That's lovely. My mum is in Poland, I call her maybe four times a week. We make pierogi together on video, she shouts at me I put too much filling.
Courtney: [laughs] Do you?
Agnieszka: Always! I'm generous. Do you sell your drawings?
Courtney: A few prints. At a zine fair in Newcastle. And I've got an Instagram, it's anonymous.
Agnieszka: Anonymous, why?
Courtney: Dunno. Easier. If people hate it, they don't know it's me.
Agnieszka: Hmm. I don't think they would hate it.
Courtney: You haven't seen it.
Agnieszka: [laughs] True! But I saw the moth on your hoodie, so I trust you.
Courtney: That's not even mine, it's from Primark.
Agnieszka: Okay, then I trust Primark.
Courtney: [laughs] Fair.

=== CALL C0233 ===
Gemma: Hiya! Oh, hello, I'm Gemma. Can you hear me all right?
Ioana: Yeah, fine. I'm Ioana.
Gemma: Ioana. Sorry, am I saying that right? I always panic with names.
Ioana: Yeah, that's right.
Gemma: Oh, good. Where are you?
Ioana: Burnt Oak. North West London.
Gemma: I'm Beeston, just outside Nottingham. We came down to London at Easter, actually, did the Natural History Museum because my daughter's obsessed with dinosaurs at the minute, and it was absolutely heaving. I think I was more stressed than she was.
Ioana: Yeah, it's always rammed. I don't really go into central.
Gemma: No, I don't blame you. Erm, what do you do, if you don't mind me asking?
Ioana: Lettings admin. At an estate agent's in Edgware.
Gemma: Ooh, okay. So, like, showing people round flats?
Ioana: No, the negotiators do viewings. I do the paperwork. Contracts, deposits, compliance. Making sure gas certificates are in date.
Gemma: Oh, but that's the bit that actually matters, isn't it? I'm a pharmacy technician, so I'm sort of the same, I'm the one checking everything before it goes out, and nobody notices unless you get it wrong, do you know what I mean?
Ioana: Yeah, exactly that. Nobody says thanks when the certificate's in date.
Gemma: No! And then one thing slips and it's all "right, who did this?"
Ioana: Yeah. Is that at a hospital?
Gemma: Yeah, a big one in Nottingham. Three days a week. I love it, honestly, but I'm one of those people who goes home and lies awake going "did I check that dose twice?" Even when I know I did. Rob says I should just let it go, but it's somebody's nan, isn't it, it's not a spreadsheet. Sorry, that got a bit deep for minute two.
Ioana: No, I do that. With deadlines. I'll wake up at three and think, did I register that deposit.
Gemma: And had you?
Ioana: Always. Every time.
Gemma: [laughs] That's it, isn't it! What gets you to sleep, then?
Ioana: Podcasts, mostly. True crime.
Gemma: Oh my God, me too! Which is a terrible idea before bed, I know. Do you listen to Casefile?
Ioana: Yeah. That one's good, it's properly researched.
Gemma: Have you tried the one with the two women who drink wine and chat about murders? Erm, I can't remember what it's called. They're dead funny.
Ioana: No, I don't like those ones, actually. They get the facts wrong and they laugh about victims. It kind of annoys me.
Gemma: [laughs] Okay, fair. That's me told.
Ioana: Sorry. I just think if you're doing it, do it properly.
Gemma: No, you're right, to be fair. I'd say that about a prescription. Do you listen on the way to work?
Ioana: On the bus, yeah. The 113. It's always late, so I get through loads.
Gemma: I listen while I batch cook on a Sunday. Chopping onions and hearing about a body in a lake. Rob thinks I'm unhinged.
Ioana: [laughs] My boyfriend thinks the same. He walks in and goes, "Is this another dead person?"
Gemma: That's exactly what Rob says! Oh, we're going to run out of time and I've talked at you the whole way, sorry.
Ioana: It's fine. Send me the wine one, I'll give it a go. Maybe.

=== CALL C0234 ===
Rowena: Hiya! Hello, can you hear me?
Agnieszka: Yes, hello! I'm Agnieszka. You can say Aga, it's easier.
Rowena: Aga! I'm Rowena. Oh, I was hoping I'd get you. I saw your shift rota on the fridge in the photo and thought, she's one of us.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Yes! Senior care assistant, care home in Yeovil. Forty-eight beds. And you?
Rowena: Nurse. Tissue viability, at the hospital in Warrington. So pressure ulcers, wounds.
Agnieszka: Oh, so you are the person we call when somebody's heels are red and we panic!
Rowena: That's me! Honestly, care homes are where it starts or stops, you know. If the carers are turning people properly and checking the skin, I've got nothing to do. You're the ones catching it.
Agnieszka: Thank you. People don't say that much. Usually it's "why is this paperwork not done." And we are short-staffed again, three long days, I'm knackered.
Rowena: Oh, three long days. You poor thing. Do you get a day off now?
Agnieszka: Tomorrow, yes. I walk the dog, Biscuit, he's Mark's, my husband's, old cocker spaniel. But if it's raining he just sits at the door and looks at me like I'm crazy.
Rowena: [laughs] Clever dog. Where are you from originally? I'm guessing not Yeovil.
Agnieszka: Rzeszów, in Poland. South-east. I came at twenty-two, so, eighteen years.
Rowena: Snap, almost! Philippines, Batangas. 2003. I shared a house with five other nurses when I first came, I cried every night for about six months.
Agnieszka: Oh, I know this feeling. First job was hotel kitchen in Somerset, I didn't know anybody. And now my mum is getting older and I'm here looking after other people's mums. It's strange, no?
Rowena: It is, yeah. My mum and dad are still in Batangas. I video call, I send money, but it's not the same as being there. Sorry, that got heavy!
Agnieszka: No, it's okay. I think everyone like us feels it. I go to Mass and I light a candle, it helps a bit.
Rowena: Me too. I sing in the Filipino choir at my parish. We've got a fiesta coming up, so it's practice every Thursday.
Agnieszka: Thursday is my Zumba! With two girls from work. It's more laughing than dancing.
Rowena: I do Zumba on Tuesdays! Our instructor plays the same five songs every week. I could do it in my sleep.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Ours too! Always "Despacito." Every week, "Despacito."
Rowena: Oh, it's the law, I think. Do you cook Polish food at home?
Agnieszka: All the time. Pierogi in big batches for the freezer. Mark says I made him half-Polish with food only.
Rowena: [laughs] My brother-in-law's the same with adobo. He's from Warrington, he'd never had rice with everything before me.
Agnieszka: And now?
Rowena: Now he asks where the rice is! We should swap recipes, Aga. Pierogi for lumpia.
Agnieszka: Yes, deal! But you have to tell me which is the best Zumba song.
Rowena: None of them. That's the answer.

=== CALL C0235 ===
Ioana: Hi. Can you hear me?
Courtney: Yeah. Hiya.
Ioana: I'm Ioana.
Courtney: Courtney.
Ioana: Where are you?
Courtney: Sunderland. You?
Ioana: North West London. Burnt Oak.
Courtney: Right.
Ioana: Yeah.
Courtney: Erm... what do you do, then?
Ioana: Lettings admin. Estate agent's in Edgware.
Courtney: No way. That's what I do. Well, part-time. Lettings and property management, in town.
Ioana: Seriously? Okay. What are you on, phones?
Courtney: Phones, booking viewings, chasing tenants for paperwork. And I scan everything into this system nobody else in the office understands. Like, I set the folders up, and now if I'm off nobody can find anything, so they just ring me. On my day off. To ask where a gas certificate is.
Ioana: [laughs] That's me. Exactly that. I'm the one who knows where everything is, and they ring me on a Saturday.
Courtney: Do the negotiators promise tenants stuff and then just leave it?
Ioana: All the time. "Oh, yeah, the landlord will definitely sort the boiler." He won't. He's never sorted anything. Then the tenant rings me and I'm the one getting shouted at, and the negotiator's out doing a viewing in his Mini.
Courtney: Ours is called Craig. He's always out doing a viewing.
Ioana: There's always a Craig.
Courtney: [laughs] Yeah.
Ioana: Do you want to stay in it? Lettings?
Courtney: Not really. It pays for stuff. I draw, that's what I actually want to do, illustration. But I'm realistic, like. I'll be scanning tenancy agreements for a bit.
Ioana: I'm doing an accounting course, AAT. So I can get into property accounts. Fewer phone calls.
Courtney: Fewer phone calls sounds amazing, ngl.
Ioana: That's honestly the main reason.
Courtney: Yeah.
Ioana: What kind of drawing?
Courtney: Ink, mostly. Kind of creepy stuff, people say. Moths and that. I read a lot of horror, so it sort of comes from there.
Ioana: I read crime. Thrillers, on the bus. Not horror, though, I can't sleep after.
Courtney: I'm the opposite, I can't sleep anyway, so I just end up on Wikipedia at two in the morning reading about unsolved stuff. Like, the Dyatlov Pass thing, have you heard of that? These hikers in Russia in the fifties who cut their way out of their tent from the inside and ran off into the snow with no shoes on, and there's about twenty theories, and I've read all of them, and none of them really work. I think that's why I like it, it doesn't finish properly.
Ioana: No, see, that would do my head in. I want to know who did it. That's why I like detective stuff, it gets solved.
Courtney: Fair. Real life doesn't, though.
Ioana: That's why I like the books.
Courtney: [laughs] Okay, that's actually a good point.
Ioana: Someone just told me about a podcast, two women drinking wine and talking about murders. I said I'd try it.
Courtney: Are you going to?
Ioana: Probably not.
Courtney: Yeah, I wouldn't.

=== CALL C0236 ===
Gemma: Hiya! Hello, I'm Gemma. Can you hear me okay?
Courtney: Yeah. Courtney.
Gemma: Courtney. Lovely. I'm in Beeston, near Nottingham. Where are you?
Courtney: Sunderland.
Gemma: Ooh, I've never been. We went to Durham once for a wedding, does that count? Probably not, sorry.
Courtney: Not really, no.
Gemma: [laughs] No, fair enough. Erm, I love your hoodie, by the way, the little moth. I noticed it in your photo.
Courtney: Thanks. It's Primark.
Gemma: Well, it's a good Primark. What do you do, are you at uni?
Courtney: No. Admin. Lettings office, part-time.
Gemma: Oh, right, sorry, I just assumed. I'm part-time as well, I'm a pharmacy technician at the hospital. Three days. Do you like it, the lettings?
Courtney: It's fine. It pays for stuff.
Gemma: That's honest! Erm, sorry, I'm going to be really nosy, were those your drawings on the wall behind you?
Courtney: Yeah.
Gemma: I thought so! I can't draw at all, I'm terrible. I've just started pottery, though, night classes, and I've got a whole shelf of mugs that lean. Like, every single one leans a bit to the left, I don't know what I'm doing with my hands. Rob says they look like they've had a drink.
Courtney: [laughs] Do you glaze them yourself?
Gemma: Yeah! That's the best bit. I did one blue and green, and it came out of the kiln sort of brown, and I was gutted.
Courtney: Glaze does that. It's like, you never really know until it's fired. I like that, though. Wonky stuff's better than shop stuff. Everything in the shops looks the same. If it leans, at least someone made it.
Gemma: Oh, that's a lovely way of putting it. I'm going to tell Rob that.
Courtney: He'll still think they're drunk.
Gemma: [laughs] He will. What do you draw, then?
Courtney: Ink stuff. Hands, moths, faces that turn into plants. I was talking to someone earlier about drawing old people's hands, actually. They're the best ones.
Gemma: Oh, I see a lot of old hands on the wards! Thin skin, all the veins. Erm, did you study it? Art?
Courtney: A-level. Started a Fine Art degree in Newcastle. Left in first year.
Gemma: Oh, I did that! Biomedical Science at Sheffield Hallam, left after first year. I still think about it, to be honest, whether I wasted it.
Courtney: Yeah. Same.
Gemma: I got there in the end, though, sort of sideways, through work. So it's not over, do you know what I mean? You're what, twenty-one?
Courtney: Yeah.
Gemma: Duck, you've got loads of time. Sorry, I sound like your mam now.
Courtney: Bit, yeah.
Gemma: [laughs] Sorry! I'll stop.
Courtney: It's fine. Send us a picture of the mugs.
Gemma: Only if you send me a moth.

=== CALL C0237 ===
Rowena: Hiya! Oh, hello! I'm Rowena. Can you hear me okay?
Ioana: Yeah. I'm Ioana.
Rowena: Ioana, lovely. Where are you, love?
Ioana: Burnt Oak. North West London.
Rowena: London! I'm Warrington. What do you do?
Ioana: Lettings admin. Estate agent's.
Rowena: Oh, I could never. All those landlords! Is it stressful?
Ioana: Kind of. It's more the phone calls. The paperwork I don't mind, I actually like that bit.
Rowena: You like paperwork? You need to come and do my inbox, honestly. I'm a nurse, wound care, and I'd rather see ten patients than write one report.
Ioana: [laughs] I'd do your inbox. I wouldn't do the wounds.
Rowena: That's fair! Sorry, I have to ask, I saw the icon on your wall in the photo. Are you Orthodox?
Ioana: Yeah. Romanian Orthodox. My mum's quite religious. I go at Easter and Christmas, mostly for her.
Rowena: I'm Catholic, Filipino Catholic, so I'm at Mass every Sunday, my mum would kill me otherwise, even from the Philippines.
Ioana: [laughs] Yeah, it's like that.
Rowena: Do you like going, though? Or is it just for your mum?
Ioana: Mostly for her. But the Easter one, the midnight service, I do like that. Everyone's holding candles and it's dark and then they sing "Hristos a înviat" and everyone passes the light along. I don't know, it's the one time I actually feel something. Even if I'm knackered.
Rowena: Oh, that gave me goosebumps. We have Simbang A5 at Christmas back home, dawn Masses, nine of them, you get up at four in the morning. Then puto bumbong outside after.
Ioana: Nine? At four?
Rowena: Nine! You get a wish if you do all of them. I never managed it.
Ioana: [laughs] I wouldn't manage one.
Rowena: Did you grow up in London, then?
Ioana: Came at eleven. From Cluj.
Rowena: Eleven, that's a hard age to move.
Ioana: Yeah. It was quite lonely, at school, for a bit. It's fine now.
Rowena: I came at twenty-eight and I still cried for six months, so you did really well. Is your family here?
Ioana: Mum, stepdad, my brother. My grandmother's still in Cluj. I should visit more.
Rowena: Oh, I know that one. My mum and dad are in Batangas. You always think, I should go more.
Ioana: Yeah. Exactly.
Rowena: Sorry, I'm asking you loads of questions, aren't I? I do that.
Ioana: It's fine. You ask normal ones.
Rowena: I'll take that! What's your grandmother's cooking like?
Ioana: Better than mine. Better than my mum's, but don't tell her.
Rowena: [laughs] My lips are sealed.

=== CALL C0238 ===
Gemma: Hiya! Oh, hello! I'm Gemma. Can you hear me?
Karen: Hello! Yes, I can hear you. I'm Karen. Sorry, I've still got my lanyard on, I keep forgetting to take it off.
Gemma: [laughs] I saw that in your photo, the badge was the wrong way round. I do exactly the same, I've gone to Tesco in mine before.
Karen: Oh, I've done Tesco in mine loads. Where are you?
Gemma: Beeston, near Nottingham. You?
Karen: Basingstoke. Not very exciting, but it's home, you know.
Gemma: Aw, no, it's nice to be from somewhere. What do you do, Karen?
Karen: Admin, at a building maintenance firm. I book the engineers in, answer the phones. I'm honestly a bit hopeless at the organising bit, to be fair, my desk is just Post-it notes. I'm better on the phone. Someone's ringing up because their ceiling's leaking and they're crying, and I'm quite good at that, calming people down, you know. It's the confirmation emails I forget.
Gemma: Oh, but the calming down is the hard bit! You can't teach that. I'm a pharmacy technician and I've got colour-coded checklists for everything, but if a nurse is stressed I'm the one going "right, okay, deep breath."
Karen: Colour-coded! I'd love that. Could you come and do my desk?
Gemma: [laughs] I would actually enjoy that, which says a lot about me.
Karen: Have you got kids? Sorry, I always ask that, I'm a mum, it just comes out.
Gemma: No, go on! One, Isla, she's six. You?
Karen: Callum, he's fourteen. Growing out of school trousers every five minutes. I bought new ones in September and they're halfway up his shins already.
Gemma: Oh no! Isla's the same with shoes. Does he go to his dad's?
Karen: Every other weekend, mostly. And my mum helps with lifts, I don't know what I'd do without her. Her knee's playing up at the minute, though.
Gemma: My mum does two pick-ups for us. I worry about her, to be honest, since my dad died. She's on her own with this mardy old Jack Russell.
Karen: Aw. I lost my dad too. You sort of keep an eye on them more, don't you?
Gemma: You do, yeah. Sorry, that got serious. Erm, do you bake? I feel like you bake.
Karen: [laughs] A Victoria sponge for birthdays. That's my one thing.
Gemma: I did a lemon drizzle for church on Sunday and it sank right in the middle. Like a crater. I filled it with icing and hoped nobody'd notice.
Karen: That's what icing's for! Did they notice?
Gemma: The vicar had two slices, so no.
Karen: There you go then. What are you having for your dinner tonight?
Gemma: Tea? Oh, it's a veggie chilli, it's in the freezer, labelled. Sorry, "tea", that's a Nottingham thing.
Karen: I'll be in Tesco at half six staring at the shelves, probably. Fajita kit, maybe.
Gemma: Honestly, that's a perfectly good tea.

=== CALL C0239 ===
Agnieszka: Hello! Hello, can you hear me?
Ioana: Yeah. Hi, I'm Ioana.
Agnieszka: Agnieszka. Or Aga, it's easier. Where are you, Ioana?
Ioana: North West London. Burnt Oak.
Agnieszka: I'm Yeovil, Somerset. I'm care assistant, senior, in a care home. And you?
Ioana: Lettings admin. Estate agent's.
Agnieszka: Ah, okay. Is that from Romania, your name? I saw an icon on your wall in the photo, I thought maybe Romanian or Orthodox.
Ioana: Yeah, both. You're the second person today who's asked about the icon.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Sorry! It's because we notice. I'm Polish, Catholic. We see a cross or icon and we think, okay, she will understand.
Ioana: That's fair. Where in Poland?
Agnieszka: Rzeszów. South-east, near Ukraine border, near the mountains. You?
Ioana: Cluj. I came here at eleven.
Agnieszka: Eleven, wow. I was twenty-two. So you are basically London girl.
Ioana: Kind of. My accent is. My mum still talks to me in Romanian though.
Agnieszka: Mine also, my mum. I call her four times a week, we cook together on video. She is in Poland, I'm here looking after other people's mums. Sometimes I think it's a bit funny. Not funny, you know, strange.
Ioana: Yeah. My grandmother's in Cluj. I try and go every year or two, but flights and everything.
Agnieszka: Which airport?
Ioana: Luton. Wizz Air. I get there about three hours early, because airports stress me out.
Agnieszka: Three hours! I thought I was bad. I go from Bristol, I make a list, I check my passport maybe ten times in the car. Mark, my husband, he says, "Aga, it's still there."
Ioana: [laughs] Liam says that. And then I check again.
Agnieszka: Do you cook Romanian food? I love sarmale, there was a Romanian lady at my work, she brought them once.
Ioana: At Christmas, yeah. My mum's are better than mine. In the week it's just normal stuff, stir fries. I do the Lidl shop on a Sunday with a list.
Agnieszka: Aldi for me. And the prices now! Every week something is more.
Ioana: Lidl's got so expensive. I've started looking at the price per kilo on everything.
Agnieszka: Yes, me too! We are the same, I think. Organised ladies.
Ioana: Probably, yeah.
Agnieszka: Sorry, I talk too much, yeah? You're very calm.
Ioana: No, it's fine. I'm just quiet at first. You're easy to talk to.
Agnieszka: Oh, thank you! That's nice.

calls.C0230:
Gemma: Hiya! Can you hear me okay? I'm never sure with this laptop, it sort of freezes if Rob's downloading anything.
Rowena: Yes, I can hear you lovely! Hiya, I'm Rowena. You're Gemma, yeah?
Gemma: That's me, yeah. Ooh, I love your glasses. Sorry, that's a weird way to start.
Rowena: No, no, I'll take it! Nobody compliments me at work, they just bleep me. Where are you, then? Are you from round here, wherever here is?
Gemma: Beeston, so just outside Nottingham. Born and bred, really. What about you?
Rowena: Warrington. Great Sankey. But originally from the Philippines, Batangas, I came over in 2003 with the nurse recruitment. Twenty years now, so I'm basically Northern.
Gemma: Oh, you're a nurse? I'm in pharmacy! I'm a pharmacy technician at the hospital in Nottingham.
Rowena: No way! NHS! What do you do, the dispensary?
Gemma: Dispensary mostly, erm, and then I go up on the wards for medicines reconciliation, so sort of checking what people are actually taking at home against what's written down. Which is never the same, do you know what I mean? Someone'll say "oh, I take the little white one" and you're like, right, okay, which little white one, there's about four hundred.
Rowena: [laughs] The little white one! I get that with creams. "The one in the blue tube, love." I'm tissue viability, so pressure ulcers, wounds, that kind of thing.
Gemma: Oh, that's a specialist job, isn't it?
Rowena: Band 7, yeah. I love it, honestly. I do a lot of teaching for the healthcare assistants and the new nurses, and I try to make it fun, because pressure ulcers on a PowerPoint, you know, people's eyes go.
Gemma: I do the training for our new starters! I've got colour-coded checklists, it's a bit of a joke in the department. They call me the highlighter lady.
Rowena: Oh, you'd hate my inbox. It's a disaster. I'd rather go and see a patient than answer an email.
Gemma: [laughs] Fair enough. Erm, sorry, I noticed in your photo, is that a choir rota on your board?
Rowena: Yes! Filipino choir at my parish. We're practising for a fiesta at the minute. Do you sing?
Gemma: I do! Church music group at the Methodist church, I'm an alto, and then a community choir that does pop stuff. We're learning a new one for a summer concert and I keep singing the soprano line by accident.
Rowena: Ah, that's lovely. I knew it, I saw your cross and thought, she'll be a singer.
Gemma: [laughs] That's very good detective work. Is it all hymns, yours, or...
Rowena: Hymns on Sunday, then at the parties it's karaoke, Whitney, Celine. No mercy.
Gemma: Oh, I'd be in tears. I cry at everything. I went to Les Mis at the Theatre Royal and Rob had to give me his sleeve.
Rowena: Me and my work friends do the Palace in Manchester. We saw Wicked and I was a mess. Do you have kids, Gemma?
Gemma: One, Isla, she's six. Dinosaurs and loom bands at the minute. My wrists are covered in them, I look like I've been to a festival.
Rowena: [laughs] I'm the fun auntie. My sister's two, Mia's fifteen, Ethan's eleven. We all live together, it's chaos but nice chaos.
Gemma: Aw, that sounds lovely, actually. My mum does two pick-ups a week for us, I'd be lost without her. Sorry, I'm rambling, aren't I?
Rowena: No, I'm the same! We're going to get told off by the timer. What do you do on a Saturday, then? I always get a barm from the bakery, that's my treat.
Gemma: A barm! See, we'd say cob. A cheese cob from the market.
Rowena: Cob! That sounds like a horse.
Gemma: [laughs] It's a perfectly good word, thank you very much!
calls.C0231:
Karen: Hello! Oh, sorry, I think I was on mute. Can you hear me now?
Ioana: Yeah, I can hear you.
Karen: Brilliant. I'm Karen. Sorry, I've still got my work lanyard on, I've literally just walked in.
Ioana: That's fine. I'm Ioana.
Karen: Ioana. Lovely name. Where are you, then?
Ioana: Burnt Oak. North West London.
Karen: Oh, not far from me, sort of. I'm Basingstoke. Well, it's not that close, is it, to be honest, it's the M3 and then a nightmare.
Ioana: Yeah, it's a way.
Karen: What do you do? Is that all right to ask? I'm not sure what we're meant to talk about.
Ioana: I think it's whatever. Erm, I'm a lettings administrator. At an estate agent's in Edgware.
Karen: Oh, so tenancies and that?
Ioana: Yeah, tenancy agreements, deposits, gas safety reminders, chasing references. Landlord statements. Basically making sure nobody gets fined.
Karen: That sounds really organised. I'm admin as well, at a building maintenance firm. I book the engineers in, chase invoices, answer the phones. But I'm hopeless, to be fair. My desk is just Post-it notes. I double-booked a plumber last month and he turned up at a job where someone else was already under the sink.
Ioana: [laughs] Okay, that's quite bad.
Karen: It was bad! I owned up, though. My manager just sort of sighed.
Ioana: Honestly, owning up is half of it. The negotiators at mine promise tenants stuff without checking, then it's me who has to sort it. They never say sorry.
Karen: That would wind me up, yeah.
Ioana: It does. I've been told to soften my emails, so.
Karen: [laughs] Soften them how?
Ioana: Like, I wrote to a landlord, "As I said in my previous three emails." And apparently that's passive-aggressive.
Karen: Well, it's a bit aggressive. But he deserved it, probably.
Ioana: He did. He emails me at eleven at night.
Karen: Oh, no. Sorry, where was I? I was going to ask, what do you do when you're not at work? That's probably a boring question, isn't it?
Ioana: No, it's fine. Erm, walking, mostly, at the weekends. Stanmore Common. And I'm doing an accounting course in the evenings, AAT.
Karen: In the evenings? After a full day? I'd be asleep on the settee by eight. I'm knackered most nights, I just put a crime drama on.
Ioana: What are you watching?
Karen: Oh, I'm halfway through this new one, the detective with the dodgy back, I can't remember the name. I binged four episodes Sunday while my son was at his dad's.
Ioana: I watch loads of those. Scandinavian ones especially. My boyfriend talks through them, so I watch them on my own.
Karen: Callum does that! My son, he's fourteen. "Who's that? Is he the killer?" Every five minutes.
Ioana: Yeah, that's Liam. And then he guesses right and he's so smug about it.
Karen: [laughs] Have you seen The Bridge?
Ioana: Yeah, the first two series are really good. Then it kind of goes off.
Karen: I never finished it. I don't really finish anything, to be honest. My mum gives me books and they just sit there.
Ioana: I read on the bus. The 113's always late, so I get loads done.
Karen: Every cloud, eh?
calls.C0232:
Agnieszka: Hello! Hello, can you see me?
Courtney: Yeah.
Agnieszka: Oh good. I'm Agnieszka. It's a hard one, people say "Agnes" sometimes, it's fine.
Courtney: Courtney.
Agnieszka: Nice to meet you, Courtney. Where are you calling from?
Courtney: Sunderland.
Agnieszka: Oh, far up! I'm in Yeovil, in Somerset. Very different, I think.
Courtney: Probably, yeah.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Okay. Erm, did you do the puzzle bit at the start? I was terrible. I think I was too slow.
Courtney: It was all right. I didn't finish the last one.
Agnieszka: Me also not! Okay, good, so not just me. I'm a care assistant, senior care assistant in a care home, so I'm used to people who can't find their glasses, not puzzles. Sorry, I talk too much, yeah? What do you do?
Courtney: Erm, admin. Lettings office. Phones and that.
Agnieszka: Do you like it?
Courtney: No. It's fine. It pays for stuff.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Honest, I like it.
Courtney: Yeah.
Agnieszka: In your photo, I saw the drawings on the wall behind you. Are they yours?
Courtney: Erm... yeah. Most of them.
Agnieszka: They looked very detailed, even small on the screen. What do you draw?
Courtney: It's kind of ink stuff, like, fineliner. Hands a lot. Moths. Faces that sort of turn into plants, like the skin goes into leaves and roots. People say it's creepy but I don't think it is, it's more like, things changing into other things. I've been doing hands for months because they're dead hard, there's loads going on in them, all the little lines and the knuckles, and if you get one bit wrong the whole thing looks like a glove. I've got this new pen, it's a point oh three, and it's... sorry. I'm going on.
Agnieszka: No, no, I like it! You know, at work I see a lot of hands. Old hands, very thin skin, all the lines. One lady, she is ninety-four, her hands are like a map. I always think somebody should draw them.
Courtney: That's actually... yeah. Old hands are the best ones to draw. My nana let me draw hers once.
Agnieszka: Ah, bless her. You're close to your nana?
Courtney: Yeah. She lives two streets away. She's the one who got me drawing, really.
Agnieszka: That's lovely. My mum is in Poland, I call her maybe four times a week. We make pierogi together on video, she shouts at me I put too much filling.
Courtney: [laughs] Do you?
Agnieszka: Always! I'm generous. Do you sell your drawings?
Courtney: A few prints. At a zine fair in Newcastle. And I've got an Instagram, it's anonymous.
Agnieszka: Anonymous, why?
Courtney: Dunno. Easier. If people hate it, they don't know it's me.
Agnieszka: Hmm. I don't think they would hate it.
Courtney: You haven't seen it.
Agnieszka: [laughs] True! But I saw the moth on your hoodie, so I trust you.
Courtney: That's not even mine, it's from Primark.
Agnieszka: Okay, then I trust Primark.
Courtney: [laughs] Fair.
calls.C0233:
Gemma: Hiya! Oh, hello, I'm Gemma. Can you hear me all right?
Ioana: Yeah, fine. I'm Ioana.
Gemma: Ioana. Sorry, am I saying that right? I always panic with names.
Ioana: Yeah, that's right.
Gemma: Oh, good. Where are you?
Ioana: Burnt Oak. North West London.
Gemma: I'm Beeston, just outside Nottingham. We came down to London at Easter, actually, did the Natural History Museum because my daughter's obsessed with dinosaurs at the minute, and it was absolutely heaving. I think I was more stressed than she was.
Ioana: Yeah, it's always rammed. I don't really go into central.
Gemma: No, I don't blame you. Erm, what do you do, if you don't mind me asking?
Ioana: Lettings admin. At an estate agent's in Edgware.
Gemma: Ooh, okay. So, like, showing people round flats?
Ioana: No, the negotiators do viewings. I do the paperwork. Contracts, deposits, compliance. Making sure gas certificates are in date.
Gemma: Oh, but that's the bit that actually matters, isn't it? I'm a pharmacy technician, so I'm sort of the same, I'm the one checking everything before it goes out, and nobody notices unless you get it wrong, do you know what I mean?
Ioana: Yeah, exactly that. Nobody says thanks when the certificate's in date.
Gemma: No! And then one thing slips and it's all "right, who did this?"
Ioana: Yeah. Is that at a hospital?
Gemma: Yeah, a big one in Nottingham. Three days a week. I love it, honestly, but I'm one of those people who goes home and lies awake going "did I check that dose twice?" Even when I know I did. Rob says I should just let it go, but it's somebody's nan, isn't it, it's not a spreadsheet. Sorry, that got a bit deep for minute two.
Ioana: No, I do that. With deadlines. I'll wake up at three and think, did I register that deposit.
Gemma: And had you?
Ioana: Always. Every time.
Gemma: [laughs] That's it, isn't it! What gets you to sleep, then?
Ioana: Podcasts, mostly. True crime.
Gemma: Oh my God, me too! Which is a terrible idea before bed, I know. Do you listen to Casefile?
Ioana: Yeah. That one's good, it's properly researched.
Gemma: Have you tried the one with the two women who drink wine and chat about murders? Erm, I can't remember what it's called. They're dead funny.
Ioana: No, I don't like those ones, actually. They get the facts wrong and they laugh about victims. It kind of annoys me.
Gemma: [laughs] Okay, fair. That's me told.
Ioana: Sorry. I just think if you're doing it, do it properly.
Gemma: No, you're right, to be fair. I'd say that about a prescription. Do you listen on the way to work?
Ioana: On the bus, yeah. The 113. It's always late, so I get through loads.
Gemma: I listen while I batch cook on a Sunday. Chopping onions and hearing about a body in a lake. Rob thinks I'm unhinged.
Ioana: [laughs] My boyfriend thinks the same. He walks in and goes, "Is this another dead person?"
Gemma: That's exactly what Rob says! Oh, we're going to run out of time and I've talked at you the whole way, sorry.
Ioana: It's fine. Send me the wine one, I'll give it a go. Maybe.
calls.C0234:
Rowena: Hiya! Hello, can you hear me?
Agnieszka: Yes, hello! I'm Agnieszka. You can say Aga, it's easier.
Rowena: Aga! I'm Rowena. Oh, I was hoping I'd get you. I saw your shift rota on the fridge in the photo and thought, she's one of us.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Yes! Senior care assistant, care home in Yeovil. Forty-eight beds. And you?
Rowena: Nurse. Tissue viability, at the hospital in Warrington. So pressure ulcers, wounds.
Agnieszka: Oh, so you are the person we call when somebody's heels are red and we panic!
Rowena: That's me! Honestly, care homes are where it starts or stops, you know. If the carers are turning people properly and checking the skin, I've got nothing to do. You're the ones catching it.
Agnieszka: Thank you. People don't say that much. Usually it's "why is this paperwork not done." And we are short-staffed again, three long days, I'm knackered.
Rowena: Oh, three long days. You poor thing. Do you get a day off now?
Agnieszka: Tomorrow, yes. I walk the dog, Biscuit, he's Mark's, my husband's, old cocker spaniel. But if it's raining he just sits at the door and looks at me like I'm crazy.
Rowena: [laughs] Clever dog. Where are you from originally? I'm guessing not Yeovil.
Agnieszka: Rzeszów, in Poland. South-east. I came at twenty-two, so, eighteen years.
Rowena: Snap, almost! Philippines, Batangas. 2003. I shared a house with five other nurses when I first came, I cried every night for about six months.
Agnieszka: Oh, I know this feeling. First job was hotel kitchen in Somerset, I didn't know anybody. And now my mum is getting older and I'm here looking after other people's mums. It's strange, no?
Rowena: It is, yeah. My mum and dad are still in Batangas. I video call, I send money, but it's not the same as being there. Sorry, that got heavy!
Agnieszka: No, it's okay. I think everyone like us feels it. I go to Mass and I light a candle, it helps a bit.
Rowena: Me too. I sing in the Filipino choir at my parish. We've got a fiesta coming up, so it's practice every Thursday.
Agnieszka: Thursday is my Zumba! With two girls from work. It's more laughing than dancing.
Rowena: I do Zumba on Tuesdays! Our instructor plays the same five songs every week. I could do it in my sleep.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Ours too! Always "Despacito." Every week, "Despacito."
Rowena: Oh, it's the law, I think. Do you cook Polish food at home?
Agnieszka: All the time. Pierogi in big batches for the freezer. Mark says I made him half-Polish with food only.
Rowena: [laughs] My brother-in-law's the same with adobo. He's from Warrington, he'd never had rice with everything before me.
Agnieszka: And now?
Rowena: Now he asks where the rice is! We should swap recipes, Aga. Pierogi for lumpia.
Agnieszka: Yes, deal! But you have to tell me which is the best Zumba song.
Rowena: None of them. That's the answer.
calls.C0235:
Ioana: Hi. Can you hear me?
Courtney: Yeah. Hiya.
Ioana: I'm Ioana.
Courtney: Courtney.
Ioana: Where are you?
Courtney: Sunderland. You?
Ioana: North West London. Burnt Oak.
Courtney: Right.
Ioana: Yeah.
Courtney: Erm... what do you do, then?
Ioana: Lettings admin. Estate agent's in Edgware.
Courtney: No way. That's what I do. Well, part-time. Lettings and property management, in town.
Ioana: Seriously? Okay. What are you on, phones?
Courtney: Phones, booking viewings, chasing tenants for paperwork. And I scan everything into this system nobody else in the office understands. Like, I set the folders up, and now if I'm off nobody can find anything, so they just ring me. On my day off. To ask where a gas certificate is.
Ioana: [laughs] That's me. Exactly that. I'm the one who knows where everything is, and they ring me on a Saturday.
Courtney: Do the negotiators promise tenants stuff and then just leave it?
Ioana: All the time. "Oh, yeah, the landlord will definitely sort the boiler." He won't. He's never sorted anything. Then the tenant rings me and I'm the one getting shouted at, and the negotiator's out doing a viewing in his Mini.
Courtney: Ours is called Craig. He's always out doing a viewing.
Ioana: There's always a Craig.
Courtney: [laughs] Yeah.
Ioana: Do you want to stay in it? Lettings?
Courtney: Not really. It pays for stuff. I draw, that's what I actually want to do, illustration. But I'm realistic, like. I'll be scanning tenancy agreements for a bit.
Ioana: I'm doing an accounting course, AAT. So I can get into property accounts. Fewer phone calls.
Courtney: Fewer phone calls sounds amazing, ngl.
Ioana: That's honestly the main reason.
Courtney: Yeah.
Ioana: What kind of drawing?
Courtney: Ink, mostly. Kind of creepy stuff, people say. Moths and that. I read a lot of horror, so it sort of comes from there.
Ioana: I read crime. Thrillers, on the bus. Not horror, though, I can't sleep after.
Courtney: I'm the opposite, I can't sleep anyway, so I just end up on Wikipedia at two in the morning reading about unsolved stuff. Like, the Dyatlov Pass thing, have you heard of that? These hikers in Russia in the fifties who cut their way out of their tent from the inside and ran off into the snow with no shoes on, and there's about twenty theories, and I've read all of them, and none of them really work. I think that's why I like it, it doesn't finish properly.
Ioana: No, see, that would do my head in. I want to know who did it. That's why I like detective stuff, it gets solved.
Courtney: Fair. Real life doesn't, though.
Ioana: That's why I like the books.
Courtney: [laughs] Okay, that's actually a good point.
Ioana: Someone just told me about a podcast, two women drinking wine and talking about murders. I said I'd try it.
Courtney: Are you going to?
Ioana: Probably not.
Courtney: Yeah, I wouldn't.
calls.C0236:
Gemma: Hiya! Hello, I'm Gemma. Can you hear me okay?
Courtney: Yeah. Courtney.
Gemma: Courtney. Lovely. I'm in Beeston, near Nottingham. Where are you?
Courtney: Sunderland.
Gemma: Ooh, I've never been. We went to Durham once for a wedding, does that count? Probably not, sorry.
Courtney: Not really, no.
Gemma: [laughs] No, fair enough. Erm, I love your hoodie, by the way, the little moth. I noticed it in your photo.
Courtney: Thanks. It's Primark.
Gemma: Well, it's a good Primark. What do you do, are you at uni?
Courtney: No. Admin. Lettings office, part-time.
Gemma: Oh, right, sorry, I just assumed. I'm part-time as well, I'm a pharmacy technician at the hospital. Three days. Do you like it, the lettings?
Courtney: It's fine. It pays for stuff.
Gemma: That's honest! Erm, sorry, I'm going to be really nosy, were those your drawings on the wall behind you?
Courtney: Yeah.
Gemma: I thought so! I can't draw at all, I'm terrible. I've just started pottery, though, night classes, and I've got a whole shelf of mugs that lean. Like, every single one leans a bit to the left, I don't know what I'm doing with my hands. Rob says they look like they've had a drink.
Courtney: [laughs] Do you glaze them yourself?
Gemma: Yeah! That's the best bit. I did one blue and green, and it came out of the kiln sort of brown, and I was gutted.
Courtney: Glaze does that. It's like, you never really know until it's fired. I like that, though. Wonky stuff's better than shop stuff. Everything in the shops looks the same. If it leans, at least someone made it.
Gemma: Oh, that's a lovely way of putting it. I'm going to tell Rob that.
Courtney: He'll still think they're drunk.
Gemma: [laughs] He will. What do you draw, then?
Courtney: Ink stuff. Hands, moths, faces that turn into plants. I was talking to someone earlier about drawing old people's hands, actually. They're the best ones.
Gemma: Oh, I see a lot of old hands on the wards! Thin skin, all the veins. Erm, did you study it? Art?
Courtney: A-level. Started a Fine Art degree in Newcastle. Left in first year.
Gemma: Oh, I did that! Biomedical Science at Sheffield Hallam, left after first year. I still think about it, to be honest, whether I wasted it.
Courtney: Yeah. Same.
Gemma: I got there in the end, though, sort of sideways, through work. So it's not over, do you know what I mean? You're what, twenty-one?
Courtney: Yeah.
Gemma: Duck, you've got loads of time. Sorry, I sound like your mam now.
Courtney: Bit, yeah.
Gemma: [laughs] Sorry! I'll stop.
Courtney: It's fine. Send us a picture of the mugs.
Gemma: Only if you send me a moth.
calls.C0237:
Rowena: Hiya! Oh, hello! I'm Rowena. Can you hear me okay?
Ioana: Yeah. I'm Ioana.
Rowena: Ioana, lovely. Where are you, love?
Ioana: Burnt Oak. North West London.
Rowena: London! I'm Warrington. What do you do?
Ioana: Lettings admin. Estate agent's.
Rowena: Oh, I could never. All those landlords! Is it stressful?
Ioana: Kind of. It's more the phone calls. The paperwork I don't mind, I actually like that bit.
Rowena: You like paperwork? You need to come and do my inbox, honestly. I'm a nurse, wound care, and I'd rather see ten patients than write one report.
Ioana: [laughs] I'd do your inbox. I wouldn't do the wounds.
Rowena: That's fair! Sorry, I have to ask, I saw the icon on your wall in the photo. Are you Orthodox?
Ioana: Yeah. Romanian Orthodox. My mum's quite religious. I go at Easter and Christmas, mostly for her.
Rowena: I'm Catholic, Filipino Catholic, so I'm at Mass every Sunday, my mum would kill me otherwise, even from the Philippines.
Ioana: [laughs] Yeah, it's like that.
Rowena: Do you like going, though? Or is it just for your mum?
Ioana: Mostly for her. But the Easter one, the midnight service, I do like that. Everyone's holding candles and it's dark and then they sing "Hristos a înviat" and everyone passes the light along. I don't know, it's the one time I actually feel something. Even if I'm knackered.
Rowena: Oh, that gave me goosebumps. We have Simbang A5 at Christmas back home, dawn Masses, nine of them, you get up at four in the morning. Then puto bumbong outside after.
Ioana: Nine? At four?
Rowena: Nine! You get a wish if you do all of them. I never managed it.
Ioana: [laughs] I wouldn't manage one.
Rowena: Did you grow up in London, then?
Ioana: Came at eleven. From Cluj.
Rowena: Eleven, that's a hard age to move.
Ioana: Yeah. It was quite lonely, at school, for a bit. It's fine now.
Rowena: I came at twenty-eight and I still cried for six months, so you did really well. Is your family here?
Ioana: Mum, stepdad, my brother. My grandmother's still in Cluj. I should visit more.
Rowena: Oh, I know that one. My mum and dad are in Batangas. You always think, I should go more.
Ioana: Yeah. Exactly.
Rowena: Sorry, I'm asking you loads of questions, aren't I? I do that.
Ioana: It's fine. You ask normal ones.
Rowena: I'll take that! What's your grandmother's cooking like?
Ioana: Better than mine. Better than my mum's, but don't tell her.
Rowena: [laughs] My lips are sealed.
calls.C0238:
Gemma: Hiya! Oh, hello! I'm Gemma. Can you hear me?
Karen: Hello! Yes, I can hear you. I'm Karen. Sorry, I've still got my lanyard on, I keep forgetting to take it off.
Gemma: [laughs] I saw that in your photo, the badge was the wrong way round. I do exactly the same, I've gone to Tesco in mine before.
Karen: Oh, I've done Tesco in mine loads. Where are you?
Gemma: Beeston, near Nottingham. You?
Karen: Basingstoke. Not very exciting, but it's home, you know.
Gemma: Aw, no, it's nice to be from somewhere. What do you do, Karen?
Karen: Admin, at a building maintenance firm. I book the engineers in, answer the phones. I'm honestly a bit hopeless at the organising bit, to be fair, my desk is just Post-it notes. I'm better on the phone. Someone's ringing up because their ceiling's leaking and they're crying, and I'm quite good at that, calming people down, you know. It's the confirmation emails I forget.
Gemma: Oh, but the calming down is the hard bit! You can't teach that. I'm a pharmacy technician and I've got colour-coded checklists for everything, but if a nurse is stressed I'm the one going "right, okay, deep breath."
Karen: Colour-coded! I'd love that. Could you come and do my desk?
Gemma: [laughs] I would actually enjoy that, which says a lot about me.
Karen: Have you got kids? Sorry, I always ask that, I'm a mum, it just comes out.
Gemma: No, go on! One, Isla, she's six. You?
Karen: Callum, he's fourteen. Growing out of school trousers every five minutes. I bought new ones in September and they're halfway up his shins already.
Gemma: Oh no! Isla's the same with shoes. Does he go to his dad's?
Karen: Every other weekend, mostly. And my mum helps with lifts, I don't know what I'd do without her. Her knee's playing up at the minute, though.
Gemma: My mum does two pick-ups for us. I worry about her, to be honest, since my dad died. She's on her own with this mardy old Jack Russell.
Karen: Aw. I lost my dad too. You sort of keep an eye on them more, don't you?
Gemma: You do, yeah. Sorry, that got serious. Erm, do you bake? I feel like you bake.
Karen: [laughs] A Victoria sponge for birthdays. That's my one thing.
Gemma: I did a lemon drizzle for church on Sunday and it sank right in the middle. Like a crater. I filled it with icing and hoped nobody'd notice.
Karen: That's what icing's for! Did they notice?
Gemma: The vicar had two slices, so no.
Karen: There you go then. What are you having for your dinner tonight?
Gemma: Tea? Oh, it's a veggie chilli, it's in the freezer, labelled. Sorry, "tea", that's a Nottingham thing.
Karen: I'll be in Tesco at half six staring at the shelves, probably. Fajita kit, maybe.
Gemma: Honestly, that's a perfectly good tea.
calls.C0239:
Agnieszka: Hello! Hello, can you hear me?
Ioana: Yeah. Hi, I'm Ioana.
Agnieszka: Agnieszka. Or Aga, it's easier. Where are you, Ioana?
Ioana: North West London. Burnt Oak.
Agnieszka: I'm Yeovil, Somerset. I'm care assistant, senior, in a care home. And you?
Ioana: Lettings admin. Estate agent's.
Agnieszka: Ah, okay. Is that from Romania, your name? I saw an icon on your wall in the photo, I thought maybe Romanian or Orthodox.
Ioana: Yeah, both. You're the second person today who's asked about the icon.
Agnieszka: [laughs] Sorry! It's because we notice. I'm Polish, Catholic. We see a cross or icon and we think, okay, she will understand.
Ioana: That's fair. Where in Poland?
Agnieszka: Rzeszów. South-east, near Ukraine border, near the mountains. You?
Ioana: Cluj. I came here at eleven.
Agnieszka: Eleven, wow. I was twenty-two. So you are basically London girl.
Ioana: Kind of. My accent is. My mum still talks to me in Romanian though.
Agnieszka: Mine also, my mum. I call her four times a week, we cook together on video. She is in Poland, I'm here looking after other people's mums. Sometimes I think it's a bit funny. Not funny, you know, strange.
Ioana: Yeah. My grandmother's in Cluj. I try and go every year or two, but flights and everything.
Agnieszka: Which airport?
Ioana: Luton. Wizz Air. I get there about three hours early, because airports stress me out.
Agnieszka: Three hours! I thought I was bad. I go from Bristol, I make a list, I check my passport maybe ten times in the car. Mark, my husband, he says, "Aga, it's still there."
Ioana: [laughs] Liam says that. And then I check again.
Agnieszka: Do you cook Romanian food? I love sarmale, there was a Romanian lady at my work, she brought them once.
Ioana: At Christmas, yeah. My mum's are better than mine. In the week it's just normal stuff, stir fries. I do the Lidl shop on a Sunday with a list.
Agnieszka: Aldi for me. And the prices now! Every week something is more.
Ioana: Lidl's got so expensive. I've started looking at the price per kilo on everything.
Agnieszka: Yes, me too! We are the same, I think. Organised ladies.
Ioana: Probably, yeah.
Agnieszka: Sorry, I talk too much, yeah? You're very calm.
Ioana: No, it's fine. I'm just quiet at first. You're easy to talk to.
Agnieszka: Oh, thank you! That's nice.

C0234.line_text: Rowena: It is, yeah. My mum and dad are still in Batangas. I video call, I send money, but it's not the same as being there. Sorry, that got heavy!
C0234.what: Rowena's voice catches slightly on 'being there'. She pauses for about a second, looks down and away from the camera, and blinks a few times behind her glasses before she smiles again and carries on.
